etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin mergō (“to dip; dip in; plunge; sink down into; immerse; overwhelm”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To combine into a whole.

quote.citation: 1791, Edmund Burke, letter to a member of the National Assembly:
quote.text: to merge all natural and all social sentiment in inordinate vanity

quote.citation: 1835 January, [Thomas De Quincey], “Samuel Taylor Coleridge. By the English Opium-eater. […]”, in William Tait, editor, Tait’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume II, number XIII, Edinburgh: William Tait […], →OCLC, page 8, column 1:
quote.text: Whig and Tory were merged and swallowed up in the transcendent duties of patriots—Englishmen—lovers of liberty.

definitions.definition: To blend gradually into something else.
The joining together of multiple sources.
